title: Screenshots Are Bad for Your Memory — Here's Why
paragraphs: What do you do when you see something important that you want to remember? Many of us would take a photo, or maybe a screenshot. But this could actually make it harder to remember — and new research may have found why.

Researchers at Binghamton University in New York wanted to see how screenshots affect memory, by examining a phenomenon known as the "photo-taking impairment effect." Previous studies have found that people often remember something less clearly when they take a picture of it, especially if they never look at it again.
To see if the same effect happens with screenshots, the researchers had people look at art on their smartphones, with only some taking screenshots.
They were then tested on what they retained — and indeed, taking screenshots impaired people's memory.

One possible explanation is "divided attention." When we take a picture or screenshot, some of our attention is diverted from what we're looking at and toward saving it. But the researchers don't think that's the main reason, because the effect persisted even when people had more time to view the artwork before or after taking a photo.

Another possible explanation is "cognitive offloading." When we save something on our phone, we rely on the device to remember it for us, and make less effort ourselves. However, the researchers say this probably isn't the reason either, because participants who were falsely told they could review their photos before being tested didn't perform any differently than those who had always expected to rely on their memory.

A third possibility is "attentional disengagement" — the idea that taking a photo or screenshot makes us unconsciously switch off from what we're looking at, so we process it less deeply from the beginning. From their results, the researchers say this is the most likely reason for the memory impairment.
So if we really want to remember something, it might be better to take notes instead, as writing things down can help us process and remember the information better as we receive it!
